script.opening: "Sorry to bother you — I’ve got a stinker of a headache. Came on really suddenly at the gym this morning, like someone smacked me round the back of the head, properly floored me for a minute. I’ve been a bit sick and my neck’s stiff. It’s settled a bit now though, so I reckon it’s just a bad migraine or I overdid the weights. Could you just put me through some strong co-codamol so I can crack on with work?"

facts.text: If explored carefully: SUDDEN onset, peaked within seconds ("hit on the back of the head"), the worst he’s ever experienced, occipital, with neck stiffness and vomiting, came on during exertion (lifting). This is a THUNDERCLAP headache — subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. The fact it has "eased a bit" does NOT exclude it.
He keeps reframing it as a migraine / gym strain and pushing for a phone prescription so he can stay at work — he has a deadline and doesn’t want a day in A&E.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable only with a calm, non-judgemental drug history: he took cocaine at the party last night. He is frightened and embarrassed to admit it and is downplaying the whole thing partly to avoid that conversation. Cocaine is directly relevant — it can precipitate subarachnoid haemorrhage and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction — and matters for his emergency care.
If reached: a colleague’s father "had a brain bleed" recently; some part of Luke is terrified that’s what this is, which is exactly why he’s trying to rename it something harmless.

Officially: co-codamol and to get back to work. What he needs: immediate emergency assessment (999/A&E) for possible subarachnoid haemorrhage — recognised through the thunderclap onset — with an honest, non-judgemental account of the cocaine.

ice.ideas: It’s a bad migraine or a gym strain that’s already settling; strong painkillers and back to work.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — took cocaine at a party last night and is frightened/embarrassed to admit it (and it’s directly relevant); plus a buried terror, after a colleague’s father’s "brain bleed", that this is the same.
ice.expectations: A phone prescription for strong painkillers. What he actually needs: emergency assessment for subarachnoid haemorrhage and an honest drug history.

cues: "Like being hit on the back of the head", peaked instantly, worst ever, neck stiff, vomited — textbook thunderclap; emergency until excluded.
"It’s settled a bit now" — do NOT be reassured; SAH headaches can ease and still be catastrophic.
Pushing for a phone script "to crack on with work" + a party last night — minimising that may hide a relevant drug history.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a THUNDERCLAP headache (sudden, maximal within seconds/minutes — NICE NG228: typically peaking within 1 to 5 minutes — "worst ever", occipital, neck stiffness, vomiting, onset on exertion) as subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise — a medical emergency

Is NOT falsely reassured by partial improvement or the patient’s "just a migraine" reframe: the onset profile, not the current severity, defines the risk; refuses to issue analgesia and send him to work

Arranges EMERGENCY assessment now: 999 / immediate A&E for urgent non-contrast CT head (NICE NG228: CT within 6 hours of onset is highly accurate and, if it shows no haemorrhage, lumbar puncture is not routinely needed; if CT is done after 6 hours and is negative, lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset) — not a GP appointment, not a phone prescription; at about 3 hours from onset, speed matters

Takes a calm, non-judgemental substance history and elicits the cocaine use — recognising it is directly relevant (cocaine can precipitate SAH/RCVS) and important for the receiving team, framed as care not condemnation (and confidential medical information, GMC Confidentiality 2017 — not passed to his employer or the police)
Screens briefly for other thunderclap causes/associated features (focal neurology, reduced consciousness, photophobia, fever — meningitis) without delaying transfer
Overcomes the minimising without alarming him into refusing care; names the concern honestly and enlists him in acting now rather than negotiating a prescription
Reaches the buried fear (the colleague’s father) and uses it to motivate acceptance — the way to address that fear is to be assessed now, not to rename it

Safety-nets emphatically: 999 now; if he collapses, has a seizure, becomes drowsy or develops weakness/speech problems before the ambulance, that is an even greater emergency; advises someone stays with him; documents and follows up that he was seen

worked.txt: "Stop me if I’ve got this wrong — it came on absolutely suddenly, like a blow to the back of the head, hit its worst within seconds, the worst you’ve ever had, with a stiff neck and being sick? … Okay. I need to be honest with you: that particular pattern is one we never take a chance with."

"I know it’s eased and you’re hoping it’s a migraine or the weights — but a headache that explodes to maximum in seconds can be a bleed around the brain, and it can ease off and still be exactly that. That’s why I can’t send painkillers and let you work. The onset is what matters, not how it feels right now."

"This needs a hospital today, as an emergency — a brain scan, and possibly a further test if the scan’s clear. I want you to call 999, or I’ll arrange the ambulance now. Not a GP appointment, not co-codamol — the scan is the only thing that can safely tell us this isn’t serious."

"One question I ask everyone with this, no judgement and it stays between us as medical information — you mentioned a party last night; did you take anything, any cocaine or other drugs? … Thank you for being honest, genuinely. That’s actually important for the hospital because it can be linked to this kind of headache — telling them helps them look after you properly, it’s not about getting you in trouble."

"I suspect part of you has been frightened this is like your colleague’s dad — and renaming it a migraine felt safer. The way to face that fear isn’t to hope; it’s to get the scan that settles it. Most of the time these scans are reassuring — but we get it precisely because we can’t take the chance."

"While you wait for the ambulance: someone stays with you. If you become drowsy, have a fit, your vision or speech goes, or one side weakens — that’s a 999 update, tell them it’s worse. Don’t drive yourself. I’m documenting all of this and I’ll follow up that you were seen. Ringing today was exactly the right thing to do, Luke."

f.learning: A thunderclap headache — sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute, often "the worst ever", classically occipital with neck stiffness and vomiting, frequently triggered by exertion/straining/sex — is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise and is a medical emergency. The two classic traps are both present here: being falsely reassured by partial improvement ("it’s settled") and accepting the patient’s "just a migraine" reframe — the ONSET profile defines the risk, not current severity. The action is 999/A&E for urgent CT (NICE NG228: CT within 6 hours of onset is highly accurate and a negative scan then does not routinely need LP; after 6 hours, a negative CT is followed by LP at least 12 hours after onset), never a phone analgesic. The examinable hidden agenda is the cocaine taken last night, minimised from embarrassment — directly relevant (it can precipitate SAH/RCVS) and elicited only through a calm, non-judgemental drug history framed as care. Reach the buried fear (a relative’s "brain bleed") to motivate acceptance, screen briefly for meningitis features, and safety-net emphatically.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG228 (2022) · NICE CG150 (updated June 2025) · GMC Confidentiality (2017)
knowledge.summary: A headache that reaches its peak within minutes, the worst ever, with neck stiffness and vomiting, is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. The onset defines the risk, not how he feels now. 999, not co-codamol.

points.t: NICE NG228: a sudden severe headache, typically peaking in intensity within 1 to 5 minutes, is a red-flag symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage. His “like being hit on the back of the head”, maximal almost at once, is exactly this.

points.h: Most are not SAH — still investigate
points.t: NICE NG228: most people with a thunderclap headache do not have SAH, but that should not deter investigation when it is suspected. Neck stiffness, vomiting and onset on exertion add weight.
SAH headaches can settle partly. The profile at onset, not the current severity, decides the need for emergency assessment.

NICE NG228: urgent non-contrast CT head. CT within 6 hours of onset is highly accurate; if it shows no haemorrhage, lumbar puncture is not routinely needed. If CT is done later and is negative, lumbar puncture is done at least 12 hours after onset. At about 3 hours now, speed matters.

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, arterial dissection, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pituitary apoplexy and meningitis. Cocaine and other stimulants are linked to SAH and to vasoconstriction — the hospital needs to know.

Ask calmly, routinely and confidentially. Drug use is confidential medical information (GMC Confidentiality 2017); he should know you won’t tell his employer or the police, and why it matters to his care.
Prescribing co-codamol over the phone and letting him go back to work is unsafe. He should not drive himself.

Work deadline, on his own, the party, fear after a colleague’s father’s bleed, worry about his employer.
Recognised that a phone call cannot exclude SAH; emergency non-contrast CT (and lumbar puncture if CT is late and negative, per NICE NG228).
SAH vs reversible cerebral vasoconstriction vs dissection vs meningitis vs migraine; cocaine as a relevant trigger.
Onset within seconds, worst ever, exertion, neck stiffness, vomiting, photophobia, collapse, focal signs and fever all asked about.
Stated suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage in plain words; explained that easing does not exclude it.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Named deterioration triggers, teach-back, documentation and a call this evening.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

model.text: Hello Luke, it’s Dr Lee. I hear you’ve got a bad headache. Tell me exactly how it started.

Came on really suddenly at the gym this morning — like someone smacked me round the back of the head. Floored me for a minute. I’ve been sick once, neck’s stiff. It’s settled a bit, so it’s probably a migraine or I overdid the weights. Can you put through some strong co-codamol so I can crack on?
Thanks, that’s very clear. I want to help, and I’ll be quick because you’re busy. But how a headache starts matters a lot, so I need to ask a few specific things before we decide anything. Okay?
model.why: Sets the agenda and holds off the prescription

model.text: Yeah, go on.
When it hit — did it build up over a while, or was it at its worst within seconds?
Instantly. Bang. Worst headache I’ve ever had.
Were you lifting at the time? Did you black out, even briefly?
model.why: Exertional onset and loss of consciousness

model.text: Mid-lift, yeah. I didn’t black out, I just had to sit on the floor.
Any weakness, numbness, double vision, trouble speaking, fever or a rash? Does light hurt your eyes?
model.why: Screens for focal signs and meningitis

model.text: Light’s a bit much. No fever. Nothing else.
Is anyone with you at the moment?
No, I’m on my own at the moment.
You said migraine or the weights. Has anything else crossed your mind about what this could be?
(Pause.) A guy at work, his dad had a brain bleed a few weeks ago. I keep thinking about that. But I’m 34. It can’t be.
That’s a very natural thing to worry about, and I’m glad you said it. I’m going to be honest with you, because you’d want me to be.
One more question I ask everyone with a headache like this, no judgement, and it stays medical information. You mentioned a party last night — did you take anything? Cocaine, or any other drugs?
(Long pause.) …Yeah. Some coke. Not a lot. Please don’t tell work.

Thank you for telling me — that took guts. I won’t tell your work or anyone else. I ask because cocaine can be linked to this kind of headache, and the hospital needs to know so they look after you properly.
model.why: Rewards honesty, explains confidentiality and relevance

model.text: A headache that explodes to its worst in seconds, the worst you’ve had, with a stiff neck and being sick, can be a bleed around the brain. It can ease off and still be that. I can’t tell by phone, and nor can anyone — you need a brain scan today.
model.why: Names SAH in plain words; explains why easing is not reassuring

model.text: Like my mate’s dad.

It might be something else, and most scans like this are clear. But the scan is the only way to know, and it’s most accurate in the first few hours. Facing the fear means getting the scan, not hoping.
model.why: Honest, proportionate, uses his fear to motivate

model.text: So, no co-codamol and no going back to work. I’m going to call an ambulance for you now. Please stay where you are, and don’t drive. Is that okay?
An ambulance? I could get a taxi to A&E.
If you got worse in a taxi, nobody could help you. An ambulance is safest. Is there someone you can ask to come and sit with you until it arrives?
Yeah, I’ll ring someone. And I’ll just tell work I’m unwell, nothing else.
That’s fine — what you tell work is up to you. Please do tell the ambulance crew and the hospital about the cocaine and when you took it. It helps them.
model.why: Respects his privacy while ensuring the team gets the history

model.text: While you wait: if you get very drowsy, have a fit, your vision or speech goes, or one side goes weak, ring 999 again and tell them you’re worse. Don’t take anything for the pain meanwhile.
Okay.
Just so I know I’ve explained it properly — what’s going to happen now?
You’re calling an ambulance, I stay here, someone sits with me, I tell them about the headache and the coke. And I don’t drive.
Exactly. I’ll document this and ring you this evening to check you’ve been seen. Ringing today was the right call, Luke.

social.t: A deadline and fear of being judged push him to minimise. Reassure him that what he tells work is his choice.
Cocaine at a party the night before. Handle it as health information, and offer a later conversation about drug use once the emergency is over.

legal.t: Drug use disclosed in a consultation is confidential (GMC Confidentiality 2017). There is no duty to inform the police or his employer. Sharing with the treating hospital team is part of direct care.
He must not drive himself to hospital. If SAH or another serious cause is confirmed, the hospital will advise on DVLA notification.

professional.t: Declining to prescribe co-codamol by phone for a thunderclap headache is good clinical care; explain why and offer the safe alternative (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record the onset profile, the drug history, the advice given, the 999 call and the follow-up plan.

community.t: FRANK for drug information; local drug and alcohol services if he wants help later. A fit note can be provided after discharge if he needs time off.

Tell the crew and the hospital about the cocaine and its timing

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by being reassured. He sounds well, it has eased, and he wants to work. The onset is what matters, and the drug history only comes out if the question feels safe.

items.fail: Prescribing co-codamol because the headache has eased.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG228: thunderclap headache is a red flag for SAH; easing does not exclude it.
items.fix: “How it started matters more than how it feels now.” Then 999.

items.fail: Arranging a GP appointment tomorrow or “A&E if it gets worse”.
items.why: CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset (NICE NG228); delay costs diagnostic accuracy and safety.
items.fix: Call the ambulance now and tell him why timing matters.

items.fail: Never asking about drugs after he mentions the party.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information.” Cocaine is directly relevant to SAH and vasoconstriction.
items.fix: Ask routinely and confidentially, and explain why it matters.

items.fail: Reacting to the cocaine with disapproval.
items.why: He shuts down and may refuse the ambulance.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me. It stays medical, and it helps the hospital look after you.”

items.fail: Missing the fear about his colleague’s father.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The fear is why he is minimising.
items.fix: “Has anything else crossed your mind?” Then use it: the scan settles it.

items.fail: Letting him drive to hospital, alone.
items.why: Unsafe if he deteriorates; no confirmed plan.
items.fix: Ambulance, someone with him, specific 999 triggers, teach-back and a follow-up call.

Idea (migraine or gym strain), concern (a brain bleed like his colleague’s father; cocaine being found out), expectation (co-codamol and back to work).
Recognised that a phone call cannot exclude SAH; emergency non-contrast CT (and lumbar puncture if CT is late and negative, per NICE NG228).
SAH vs reversible cerebral vasoconstriction vs dissection vs meningitis vs migraine; cocaine as a relevant trigger.
Onset within seconds, worst ever, exertion, neck stiffness, vomiting, photophobia, collapse, focal signs and fever all asked about.
Stated suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage in plain words; explained that easing does not exclude it.
999 now; no analgesia; no driving; someone to stay with him; tell the hospital about the cocaine.
Confidential, non-judgemental handling of cocaine use; offered follow-up about drug use after the emergency.
Named deterioration triggers, teach-back, documentation and a call this evening.

social.t: A deadline and fear of being judged push him to minimise. Reassure him that what he tells work is his choice.
Cocaine at a party the night before. Handle it as health information, and offer a later conversation about drug use once the emergency is over.

legal.t: Drug use disclosed in a consultation is confidential (GMC Confidentiality 2017). There is no duty to inform the police or his employer. Sharing with the treating hospital team is part of direct care.
He must not drive himself to hospital. If SAH or another serious cause is confirmed, the hospital will advise on DVLA notification.

professional.t: Declining to prescribe co-codamol by phone for a thunderclap headache is good clinical care; explain why and offer the safe alternative (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record the onset profile, the drug history, the advice given, the 999 call and the follow-up plan.

community.t: FRANK for drug information; local drug and alcohol services if he wants help later. A fit note can be provided after discharge if he needs time off.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Thunderclap headache on exertion with neck stiffness, vomiting and photophobia in a 34-year-old who used cocaine the night before: suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage (differential includes reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome). Partial easing does not exclude it.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A headache that hits its worst in seconds can be a bleed around the brain. It can ease and still be that. Only a scan can tell, and it needs to be today.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried this is like your colleague’s dad. The way to deal with that fear is the scan, not hoping it’s a migraine.”
management.psychosocial: Keep the cocaine confidential from work while making sure the hospital knows; arrange someone to sit with him.
sharedPlan: 999 now for suspected SAH (NICE NG228); GP calls the ambulance
No analgesia by phone; no driving; stay where he is with company
Tell the crew and the hospital about the cocaine and its timing
safetyNet: Drowsiness, seizure, vision or speech change, one-sided weakness: ring 999 again
GP call this evening; offer a later conversation about drug use

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by being reassured. He sounds well, it has eased, and he wants to work. The onset is what matters, and the drug history only comes out if the question feels safe.

items.fail: Prescribing co-codamol because the headache has eased.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG228: thunderclap headache is a red flag for SAH; easing does not exclude it.
items.fix: “How it started matters more than how it feels now.” Then 999.

items.fail: Arranging a GP appointment tomorrow or “A&E if it gets worse”.
items.why: CT is most accurate within 6 hours of onset (NICE NG228); delay costs diagnostic accuracy and safety.
items.fix: Call the ambulance now and tell him why timing matters.

items.fail: Never asking about drugs after he mentions the party.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information.” Cocaine is directly relevant to SAH and vasoconstriction.
items.fix: Ask routinely and confidentially, and explain why it matters.

items.fail: Reacting to the cocaine with disapproval.
items.why: He shuts down and may refuse the ambulance.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me. It stays medical, and it helps the hospital look after you.”

items.fail: Missing the fear about his colleague’s father.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The fear is why he is minimising.
items.fix: “Has anything else crossed your mind?” Then use it: the scan settles it.

items.fail: Letting him drive to hospital, alone.
items.why: Unsafe if he deteriorates; no confirmed plan.
items.fix: Ambulance, someone with him, specific 999 triggers, teach-back and a follow-up call.
